hints: Work done by a constant force is $W = Fd\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the force and the displacement.
walkthrough:
Calculate the work done by the pulling force using $W = Fd\cos\theta$:
$$W = (50\cos 10^\circ)(20) = 1000\cos 10^\circ \approx 984.8\text{ J}$$
teacher_walkthrough:
The formula for work done by a constant force inclined at angle $\theta$ to the direction of motion is:
$$W = Fd\cos\theta$$

Substitute the pulling force $F = 50\text{ N}$, distance $d = 20\text{ m}$, and angle $\theta = 10^\circ$:
$$W = 50 \times 20 \times \cos 10^\circ = 1000\cos 10^\circ$$
$$W \approx 1000 \times 0.984808 = 984.808\text{ J} \approx 984.8\text{ J}$$

hints: Apply the work-energy principle: work done by the pulling force equals kinetic energy gained plus work done against resistance.
Calculate work done against resistance: $W_{\text{res}} = 30 \times 20 = 600\text{ J}$.
walkthrough:
Set up the work-energy equation:
$$W_{\text{pull}} = \Delta E_k + W_{\text{res}}$$

Substitute $W_{\text{pull}} = 984.8\text{ J}$, $m = 25\text{ kg}$, and $W_{\text{res}} = 30 \times 20 = 600\text{ J}$:
$$984.8 = \frac{1}{2}(25)v^2 + 600 \implies 12.5 v^2 = 384.8$$

Solve for speed $v$:
$$v^2 = \frac{384.8}{12.5} = 30.784 \implies v = \sqrt{30.784} \approx 5.55\text{ m s}^{-1}$$
teacher_walkthrough:
By the work-energy theorem, the work done by the external pulling force is converted into kinetic energy and work done overcoming resistance:
$$W_{\text{pull}} = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 + W_{\text{resistance}}$$

Calculate work done against the constant resistance force of $30\text{ N}$ over $20\text{ m}$:
$$W_{\text{resistance}} = 30 \times 20 = 600\text{ J}$$

Substitute the values into the work-energy equation:
$$984.8 = \frac{1}{2}(25)v^2 + 600$$
$$984.8 = 12.5v^2 + 600$$

hints: Power is given by $P = F_x \times v$, where $F_x = 50\cos 10^\circ$ is the forward component of the force.
The force exerts its greatest power at the instant of maximum speed ($v = 5.548\text{ m s}^{-1}$).
walkthrough:
Calculate the greatest power using $P = (F\cos\theta)v_{\max}$ at the end of the $20\text{ m}$ run:
$$P = (50\cos 10^\circ)(5.548) \approx 49.240 \times 5.548 \approx 273\text{ W}$$
teacher_walkthrough:
The instantaneous power exerted by a force $F$ acting at angle $\theta$ to velocity $v$ is:
$$P = (F\cos\theta) \times v$$
Because the forward pulling force component $50\cos 10^\circ$ is constant, power is maximized when speed $v$ is greatest.
Maximum speed occurs at the end of the $20\text{ m}$ distance, where $v \approx 5.5483\text{ m s}^{-1}$:

hints: Apply Newton's second law along the $5^\circ$ slope: the forward force is $50\cos 10^\circ$, opposed by resistance ($30\text{ N}$) and downhill weight component ($25g\sin 5^\circ$).
Use $v = u + at$ with initial speed $u = 5.548\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and final speed $v = 0$ to find time $t$.
walkthrough:
Apply Newton's second law parallel to the inclined plane in the upward direction:
$$50\cos 10^\circ - 30 - 25g\sin 5^\circ = 25a$$
$$49.240 - 30 - 250\sin 5^\circ = 25a \implies 19.240 - 21.789 = 25a \implies -2.549 = 25a$$

Use $v = u + at$ with initial speed $u = 5.548\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and final speed $v = 0$:
$$0 = 5.548 - 0.1020t \implies t = \frac{5.548}{0.1020} \approx 54.4\text{ s}$$
teacher_walkthrough: On the inclined plane of angle $5^\circ$, sum the forces along the line of greatest slope in the upward direction.

The upward driving component from the pulling force is $50\cos 10^\circ$. The opposing forces are the resistance force of $30\text{ N}$ and the component of weight down the slope $mg\sin 5^\circ$:
$$F_{\text{net}} = 50\cos 10^\circ - 30 - mg\sin 5^\circ$$

Apply Newton's second law $F_{\text{net}} = ma$:
$$-2.5486 = 25a \implies a = \frac{-2.5486}{25} = -0.10194\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

The initial speed on the slope is $u \approx 5.5483\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and the final speed when coming to rest is $v = 0$. Use $v = u + at$:
$$0 = 5.5483 + (-0.10194)t$$
$$0.10194t = 5.5483$$
$$t = \frac{5.5483}{0.10194} \approx 54.43\text{ s} \approx 54.4\text{ s}$$
